extracted.intended_audience: aspiring writers, young poets, magazine contributors, and editors
extracted.subtask_description: Practical counsel for young writers and versifiers about getting published, improving craft, and interacting with editors; also guidance for editors on selection responsibilities. Contains norms about originality, timing of publication, and the proper attitude toward praise and charity in publishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Produce genuinely good work (originality and substance)
rubrics_metrics.description: If you have the consciousness of genius, do something to show it. Produce anything really good, and an intelligent editor will jump at it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The world quickly catches true originality; editors will find you. Of a hundred pieces received, ninety are at or below the sea-level; some have 'water enough, but no head; some head enough, but no water; only two or three are from full reservoirs.' Do the prettiest thing you can and wait your time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not aim chiefly at fame; focus on the work
rubrics_metrics.description: Fame usually comes to those who are thinking about something else; nothing is so commonplace as to wish to be remarkable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'struggle for fame' commonly ends in notoriety; rather than scheming for celebrity, concentrate on producing substantial work ('do something to show it').

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors prioritize quality over author notoriety or poverty
rubrics_metrics.description: An editor is a person under a contract with the public to furnish them with the best things he can afford for his money; charity shown by publication of an inferior article is improper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors must reject unfit productions even when sympathetic to the contributor's circumstances. Publishing as a form of charity would betray the public trust ('like the generosity of Claude Duval... who robbed the rich to relieve the poor'). There is always a dearth of really fine articles for a first-rate journal; nothing pleases an editor more than getting something worth having from a new hand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verse-writing carries a presumptive handicap—overcome it by demonstrable quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Verse-writers are by far the most exacting and restless literary persons; there is a presumption against young versifiers because 'there are at least nine chances in ten that he writes poor verses.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To dispel the presumption, a young poet must convince readers that the verses are worth writing. Study good models; make verse an incidental occupation rather than an all-consuming identity; avoid hasty printing. 'Not the least use in all this' unless the work shows real merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid hasty publication; delay until workmanship justifies printing
rubrics_metrics.description: There should be no hurry in printing what is written. Not the least use in rushing to print; writing should be well-polished before exposing it to public judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author counsels study of good models and patience: 'Do the prettiest thing you can and wait your time.' A 'poetaster who has tasted type is done for'—once one has printed prematurely the delusion often persists.

rubrics_metrics.name: When giving criticism, be honest but gentle with novices
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who ask your opinion often really want praise; one should be tender with young persons yet not lie about their deficiencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Soften the 'ugly central fact' of incompetence when dealing with adolescents—offer counsel (study models, make verse incidental, avoid haste) rather than blunt cruelty. Balance compassion with the duty to be candid: 'One doesn’t like to be cruel—and yet one hates to lie.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors must develop professional detachment and resist sentimental interventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors need 'enormous calluses' at points of contact with authors; their business is a matter of intellect, not sympathy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When appealed to on behalf of needy writers who hope to live by the pen, editors should evaluate manuscripts by merit. Accepting inferior work out of pity is self-defeating and contrary to the editor's obligation to readers.
